node.title: Desktop entry (main)
node.description: Binary entry point. Builds the 1400x900 Workbench window, injects style.css into the page head and launches the Dioxus desktop runtime with the App root component.

node.title: App root & header
node.description: Root component. Resolves the working directory from argv[1] or the current dir, optionally opens a file from argv[2], provides AppState as context, starts the session loop of every saved agent and creates the sessions and agents other parts of the app ask for. It reloads .workbench data when cwd or repo_version changes. The header has the graph toggle, folder picker (rfd), the provider and model picker, model and cost badges, a warning badge in Full auto mode, a branch picker and a New session button. The branch picker shows the current branch and opens a filterable list of local and remote branches; picking one runs git switch (remote-only branches get a local tracking branch), and typing a new name offers to create it, which also starts a new chat session. New session starts a chat session in the open folder. open_folder switches the working folder (used by the folder picker and the project view) and the chat to a session in it, or to no chat when the folder has none, and a project chip in the header jumps to the project that contains the open folder. The header also shows the self-updater's button when a newer build is available on GitHub.

node.title: AppState (signals store)
node.description: Central reactive store made of Dioxus signals: graph, baseline, rules, related GitHub repos, the MCP servers (the user's and the project's) and their last reported status, the user's provider settings, the projects list and whether the project view is showing, selection, the module scope path (which network the graph view shows), the chat sessions with every agent's live Chat and which one the chat shows, open file, tabs and the active job. It also holds the domain actions: open/save/revert files, load and sync the workbench from disk, update and save the graph or the current network, enter and leave modules, compute changes against the baseline, revert node and module changes, mark the graph as in sync, and update rules, related repos and MCP connections (saving MCP connections restarts Workbench on the next message). For plain chat turns of an agent in the open folder it snapshots the graph when the turn starts and, when the turn succeeds, moves the graph edits Workbench made into the baseline (the whole graph if it was in sync, otherwise only Workbench's changes), so they don't show up as the user's pending changes. Edits the user makes in the graph during the turn stay pending. Only one agent's turn or job is tracked at a time. Also defines the Cmd enum sent to the session loop.

node.title: Workbench session loop
node.description: One long-running loop per agent that receives that agent's Cmd values (Send, Prompt, Interrupt, Restart, Resume, Close; Close stops the agent and ends the loop) and owns its live agent, so agents in a session work at the same time. With Workbench it spawns the agent process lazily in the agent's folder, respawns it when the rules version changes, and resumes the agent's stored session id. A generation counter drops events from killed processes. Streamed events become the agent's chat items; when the agent works in the open folder, file-touching tool results bump repo_version and reload the open file, and Done settles its chat turn or graph job against the baseline. A reply that ends with spawn-agent blocks starts those agents with their tasks: in the same session, or, when a block names a repository of the agent's project, in a new session in that repository. A project-level agent gets the project's repositories as its context instead of the open folder's graph. Changing a project's repositories or descriptions also restarts Workbench with the updated project context. When it spawns the agent it passes the enabled MCP connections as --mcp-config, and the MCP statuses from the agent's init event go to app-state. With any other provider every message starts a new turn through the agent layer, and only Workbench session ids are saved for resuming. Each agent runs on its own provider and model when it was started on one (AppState::agent_provider), otherwise on the ones in the settings; a spawn-agent block can name a provider and model for the new agent, and an unknown provider id is shown as an error instead of starting it.

node.title: Workbench agent process
node.description: Finds the agent binary, then spawns it with stream-json input/output, partial messages, the permission mode of the chat mode, AskUserQuestion turned off (the agent asks in its reply instead), an optional --resume, --model, --append-system-prompt and --mcp-config. It writes user messages, interrupt control requests and permission answers (a plan approval also sets the session's mode) to stdin. Stdout lines are parsed into AgentEvent values (Init with the MCP server statuses, TextDelta, ToolUse, ToolResult, Done, Stderr, Exited) and tagged with a generation number. Also provides tool summaries and file-path extraction.

node.title: Workbench agent CLI
node.description: The external agent executable, run as a subprocess in the project directory. It does the actual agent work (reading and editing files, writing .workbench/graph.json) and streams JSON events back.

node.title: Prompt builder
node.description: Builds every structured prompt sent to Workbench: generate or refresh the architecture graph (with the JSON schema, including modules), draft nodes into the network the user is looking at, process graph changes into code edits (new, removed and edited modules and attachments included; Workbench may add nodes for new units it had to create, and is told which nodes and files other branches are also changing), debug a flow (several modes), audit code against rules, ask about a node, review a pull request, and the per-session system-prompt append, which tells Workbench to keep the graph in step with every code change (files, new nodes for new units, removed nodes, updated descriptions and links), plus, when the open folder belongs to a project, the project's name and the other repositories (folder, GitHub name, description) Workbench may read, the modules guide, enabled rules and the related GitHub repositories. Every agent is also told how to start more agents in its session: a spawn-agent block with a name and the full task, which spawn_requests parses out of the reply. It also builds the project-level agent's prompt (the project and its repositories) and the spawn-agent instructions, which name the project's repositories an agent can start another agent in. The spawn-agent instructions also list every provider id with its models, so when the user names a provider or model in the chat ("use vibe large 4 to build X") the agent adds provider and model to the block.

node.title: Graph model
node.description: Serde types Node, Flow, Module and Graph, plus helpers: lookup, unique ids, slugify, node removal, edges, auto-layout into columns, kind colours, and diff(base, current), which produces field-level Change records. A Module is an isolated node network stored in graph.modules; a node whose `module` field names it is an attachment point, and one module can be attached in many places (never inside itself). The diff covers the main network, every module network and module title/description, tagging each change with its scope. absorb applies a set of changes from a current graph onto a baseline. load and save read and write the graph JSON under .workbench.

node.title: Rules model
node.description: Project rules (id, title, body, enabled, optional node scope) stored in .workbench/rules.json. Provides load and save, id generation, filtering of rules relevant to a set of nodes, and rendering rules as prompt text.

node.title: .workbench data files
node.description: On-disk JSON store in the opened project: graph.json (the current, editable graph), graph.baseline.json (the last state in sync with the code) and rules.json. These files are read on load and re-read whenever the repo version changes.

node.title: Project working tree
node.description: The opened folder's source files and git repository. The editor and Workbench both read and write files here, and git commands run against it.

node.title: Graph tab & toolbar
node.description: Hosts the canvas with the floating chat and, on its right, the node menu with the Node, Flows, Changes, History and Prompt panes. The toolbar adds nodes and starts a Generate job, which sends the mapping prompt to Workbench with the graph locked until the job finishes. The nodes have draggable inputs and outputs so they're easily able to change their links. The breadcrumb row always shows project › repository › modules, and Up from the repository root opens the project view. The node menu can be hidden and resized by dragging the splitter to its left; its width and open state are saved in the workbench layout.

node.title: Prompt pane (add nodes from prompt)
node.description: Graph sub-tab where the user describes behaviour in plain text. Add nodes starts a Draft job that asks Workbench to extend graph.json with new nodes, links and flows without touching source code. Because a Draft job never updates the baseline, the new nodes show up as pending changes that are committed into code afterwards.

node.title: Chat modes (Plan / Accept edits / Auto / Full auto)
node.description: One mode decides both how the agent acts and what it may do without asking; the toggle sits under the chat and every session starts in Plan. Plan is read only: Workbench runs in its own plan mode and presents its plan with ExitPlanMode, which Workbench turns into a prompt asking whether to run it in Auto, Full auto or Accept edits, or keep planning; picking a mode answers the request and switches the running session's mode. Other providers get plan instructions instead, and their plan-mode reply gets the same prompt, which then asks them to implement the plan. Accept edits asks before every change and command, Auto answers every permission request itself except deleting files, and Full auto never asks. For Draft and Process jobs, Plan mode also lets Workbench ask numbered questions ending in a marker, pausing the job until the user answers.

node.title: Graph canvas
node.description: SVG and HTML node diagram with pan, zoom, fit-to-view, node dragging (saves the position) and link creation by clicking. It highlights the active flow path and colours nodes by kind. It always shows one network: the main graph or the module the user has opened. Module attachment nodes are drawn with a double teal border, the module name and node count, and are marked edited when their module has pending changes; double-clicking one opens the module, and a breadcrumb bar leads back up. The toolbar's + Module… menu creates a new module or attaches an existing one here. A press in the canvas or on a node fades the floating chat.

node.title: Node inspector
node.description: Editor for the selected node's title, kind, description, files and links. It shows incoming callers, can revert the node to the baseline, and has an Ask Workbench action that sends a node-specific question. Here a node holds a explicit list of links to other nodes. One list of inputs flows and one for output flows. The nodes also hold a list of the files that is related to it and in what manner, like its own dependencies, where its used and such. For reference nodes it shows the source, its detected type, whether it is a Workbench project, and a picker for the referenced project's nodes.

node.title: Changes pane (commit graph)
node.description: Lists the field-level differences between the current graph and the baseline, including nodes inside modules (labelled with their module) and added, removed or edited modules. Show opens the right module and selects the node. Before processing it reads the claims of the other git branches and warns when they change the same nodes or files, or nodes these changes depend on; the user can process anyway or process only the changes no other branch touches. With an optional note, it sends a Process job that asks Workbench to change the code to match the edited graph. When the job succeeds, the baseline is updated.

node.title: Flows pane & debug
node.description: Lists flows, lets the user draft new ones by clicking nodes in order, and highlights the active flow on the canvas. Runs a debug prompt for a flow in the chosen DebugMode, with an optional symptom description.

node.title: Rules view
node.description: CRUD list of project rules: add, edit, enable or disable, scope to a node, delete, and filter. An Audit action asks Workbench to check the codebase against all enabled rules. Any change bumps rules_version, which restarts the Workbench process on the next message.

node.title: Chat pane
node.description: Conversation view of the agent the chat shows: user messages, labelled prompts, streaming assistant markdown, tool calls with results, info lines and errors. The input box sends Cmd::Send and has a Stop button for Cmd::Interrupt while busy. ChatTabs, in the chat's top bar next to “Chat”, shows the session's title and one tab per agent with its provider's logo (and a dot while it works and ! while it waits for an answer); clicking a tab switches the chat to that agent, hovering it shows an ✕ on its left that closes the agent (closing the last one closes the session), and + adds an agent. In a project view the session title in the top bar is a session picker: the project's own sessions, every session in its repositories and their worktrees, and + New project session. Picking a repository's session shows it without leaving the project view.

node.title: Code pane (Files / Editor / Diff)
node.description: Right-hand tabs. Files lists changed files with their git status, then all files as the project's folder tree with folders that open and close on click (open folders are kept in AppState, and typing in the filter opens every folder with a match). Diff shows a syntax-highlighted git diff against a chosen base, and each hunk has an Ask Workbench button that pastes it into the chat input. Editor hosts the CodeMirror view. The GitHub tab hosts the GitHub module, the MCP tab hosts the MCP module, and the Providers tab hosts the LLM providers module.

node.title: CodeMirror editor bridge
node.description: Mounts the bundled CodeMirror 6 editor (vim mode, many languages) in the webview through document.eval. Load and focus messages go to JS; Change, Save (:w), Close (:q) and Reload (:e) messages come back and update the open file in AppState.

node.title: Git service
node.description: Thin wrapper over the git CLI: repo detection, current branch, branch listing, switching and creating branches, porcelain status, ls-files, pushing the current branch, and a diff against a base that includes untracked files. It parses the output into FileDiff, Hunk and DiffLine values, and each hunk can be turned back into a patch. For the node history it reads git log -p of the history file and maps each entry's uid to the commit, reachable from HEAD, that first added its line. For coordination it lists the authors and changed files of a branch since it split from HEAD, detects unmerged files and stages resolved ones.

node.title: Build & install tooling
node.description: Makefile targets for run, test, install, open, uninstall and the editor bundle build. install.sh builds a release binary, packages it as ~/Applications/Workbench.app and installs a `wbrs` launcher in ~/.local/bin. `make editor` uses esbuild to bundle editor-js into src/editor.bundle.js. Before building it checks for git, curl, cargo and, on Linux, make, a C compiler, pkg-config and the GUI libraries. It lists what's missing with the exact install commands (pacman, apt, dnf, zypper, apk or xbps; rustup for Rust; Xcode Command Line Tools on macOS) and runs them only after the user confirms on the terminal. It stops with an explanation on Debian/Ubuntu releases too old to have WebKitGTK 4.1. If the folder isn't a git checkout (a ZIP download), it offers to link it to the GitHub repo so the update check works, stashing any files that differ from main.

node.title: Workbench layout
node.description: The window body under the header: the projects sidebar on the left and the workbench on the right. The workbench switches between the Graph, Code and Rules views, shows workbench load errors, and shows the project view when a project is picked. The layout (sidebar open, node menu width and open state, chat anchor, expanded and locked) is saved in ~/.config/workbench/layout.json.

node.title: GitHub (PRs & repos)
node.description: The Code pane's GitHub tab. Here the module is used interactively: list, read, review, comment on, open and merge pull requests, and browse related repositories.

node.title: GitHub (related repos context)
node.description: The prompt builder uses the module's related-repository list so every Workbench session knows which other GitHub projects it may read with gh for context.

node.title: External references
node.description: Nodes of kind `reference` point outside the project through `reference.source`: a local folder or file, a GitHub repository (URL, owner/repo or github:owner/repo@ref/path), a website, or an npm/crate/pypi/go package. Sources are parsed into a Source, and Workbench looks for the referenced project's .workbench/graph.json: locally by walking up from the path, on GitHub through gh at the path and its parents, or in node_modules and the cargo registry for packages. Loaded graphs are cached in AppState by source. The user can pick nodes of that graph into `reference.nodes`, and their descriptions and files are put into the system prompt, the selection context and process prompts as read-only context.

node.title: Module inspector
node.description: Shown in the Node sub-tab when a module is open and no node is selected. Edits the module's title and description, lists every place the module is attached (click to jump there), shows pending module changes with Revert, and deletes the module together with its attachment nodes.

node.title: Ghost branches
node.description: Shows the graph work on other git branches as read-only ghost nodes on the canvas. For each branch the user picks from the Ghosts toggle, or every branch with unmerged work when they press Team, it reads the branch's .workbench/graph.json and the one at the merge base with HEAD, and diffs them so only that branch's own work appears: added nodes become dashed ghosts with dashed links, and nodes it changed or removed get a coloured ring. Each branch is labelled with the people who committed to it. A node with pending local edits that a branch also changes or depends on gets a warning ring that says the branch invalidates the edit. Clicking a ghost puts it into Workbench's context next to the selected nodes, with a note to read its code via git show instead of checking the branch out.

node.title: Project view (related repositories)
node.description: The level above a repository's graph. A project, such as Workbench, groups the local clones of the repositories that make up one product, for example frontend, backend and host. It shows each repository as a node with an editable description text box beside it instead of links, plus its graph size and GitHub remote. Projects are stored in ~/.config/workbench/projects.json and listed in the projects sidebar; the inspector sits on the right and the floating chat sits over the canvas; double-clicking a repository opens it as the working folder and shows its graph. When the open folder belongs to a project, the other repositories and their descriptions go into Workbench's system prompt.

node.title: Node history
node.description: Shared, append-only history of node and module changes (title, kind, module, reference, links, files and description) stored as before/after text. Each entry has a unique id, a time, an author (git user.name) and a source: a person in Workbench, Workbench working for that person, or an edit outside Workbench. The log is .workbench/node-history.jsonl, one entry per line, with a .workbench/.gitattributes union-merge rule so logs from several people merge without conflicts; on load lines are de-duplicated by id and sorted by time. What this client last saw of the graph is kept locally in ~/.config/workbench/node-snapshots/, and a change already in the shared log (for example pulled from a teammate) is not logged again. Rapid edits by the same person are merged into one entry, and a built-in LCS line diff renders entries as classic +/− diffs.

node.title: History pane
node.description: Bottom-panel tab that lists recorded node and module changes newest first as classic line diffs, with who made each change (you, a teammate, Workbench, or outside Workbench) and when. When one node is selected (or a module is open) it can filter to just that node's history, and Show jumps to the node. The node inspector links here with a History (n) button. There is no clear action because the log is shared with the repo. In a git repository the list is grouped against the git state: an Uncommitted section first, for entries not yet in a commit on this branch, then one section per commit (short hash, subject, author, time), newest first. Each entry also carries an uncommitted or commit-hash tag.

node.title: Self-updater
node.description: Checks on startup whether GitHub's main branch has commits that the running build lacks. It compares the commit embedded at build time (build.rs) with main through the GitHub compare API using curl. If main is ahead, a header button opens and lists the new commits. Choosing Update fetches main into a private checkout under ~/.cache/workbench/source and builds it in the background. Restart now runs that checkout's install script in a detached process and reopens the current folder. If git or cargo is missing, it points the user to install.sh instead of starting the build.

node.title: MCP connections
node.description: The Code pane's MCP tab and the MCP servers every provider can call. The user manages MCP servers at two levels in the tab: their own servers, used in every project, and the project's servers. Every active one goes to Workbench Code (--mcp-config), Codex (-c mcp_servers) or Vibe (VIBE_MCP_SERVERS), and the API providers call them through Workbench's own MCP manager. The reported connection status is shown back in the tab. Remote servers that use OAuth (such as Linear) are signed in from the tab, and each turn passes their token on as a header.

node.title: Agent layer
node.description: One interface over every LLM provider for the session loop. Workbench runs as the long-lived agent process; every other provider runs one turn per message, either a fresh Codex or Vibe process that resumes the previous session or one API request with the conversation so far, plus one more per round of MCP tool calls the model makes. All of them report back as the same chat events. Only Workbench can be interrupted mid-turn or ask for permissions; other turns are stopped by killing them.

node.title: LLM providers
node.description: Lets the user switch the chat between Workbench Code, Codex and Mistral Vibe (agent CLIs) and the Anthropic, OpenAI, Mistral and OpenRouter APIs, with a model per provider. The header uses it for the provider and model picker, the Code pane for the Providers tab, and the agent layer to run Codex, Vibe and API turns. The provider picked in the settings is only the default: an agent can be started on another provider and model from the chat through a spawn-agent block, and the chat tab, sidebar row and mode toggle show the agent's own provider.

node.title: Projects sidebar
node.description: Collapsible list on the left of every project with its repositories and worktrees, read from the projects saved in ~/.config/workbench/projects.json. Under each repository and worktree it lists its chat sessions, with a dot while one of their agents works and a ✕ on hover that closes the session; clicking the name of the open session renames it. Any session can be closed, and a folder without sessions shows a New session button instead. Under each session it lists its agents with their provider's logo and name and their state (working, waiting, or needs you when a permission or plan waits for an answer). Clicking a session or an agent opens its folder and shows it in the chat. Under each project it also lists coding agents running outside Workbench, with their provider's logo, the folder they run in and whether they are working or waiting for a prompt. Clicking a project shows its project view; clicking a repository, worktree or agent opens that folder. It can create a project and add a repository to a project. A project's project-level sessions are listed right under its name. Each project, repository, worktree and session with agents has a ▾ in front of it that folds away the rows under it; the folded rows are saved in ~/.config/workbench/sidebar_collapsed.json.

node.title: Floating chat dock
node.description: The chat floats over the graph, code or rules view, at the bottom centre until it is first moved. Dragging its top bar moves it anywhere in the window, even partly past the right and bottom edges, as long as the bar stays in the window; dragging its edges resizes it, and the place and size are saved. A press in the graph fades the chat to a peek at the latest reply unless the Lock toggle is on. Detach moves the chat into a window of its own and Attach puts it back; on macOS, detaching from a full-screen window leaves full screen first. Its top bar holds the agent tabs of the chat session it shows; when the open folder has no session it shows a New session button instead.

node.title: Agent activity
node.description: Finds the coding agents (Workbench Code, Codex, Vibe) running on this machine outside Workbench by reading /proc, which folder each runs in, and whether it is working (using CPU) or waiting for a prompt. Every agent is given to the project repository or worktree it runs in; Workbench's own agents are shown with their chat sessions instead. Each agent kind and each provider maps to its LLM company's logo (Claude, OpenAI, Mistral, OpenRouter), drawn from Simple Icons path data. The worktree list in the project view can add a worktree, which also starts a new chat session in it.

node.title: Theme & dropdowns
node.description: theme.css holds every colour, radius, font and shadow as a CSS variable, plus the base control styles; style.css only uses these variables. The webview draws native <select> and <datalist> popups with the system theme, so dropdown.rs draws themed ones instead: Dropdown picks one of a list of choices, and ComboBox is a text field with suggestions, used for model names and node kinds. Their open list is fixed to the window and opens upwards when there is more room above.

node.title: Chat sessions & agents
node.description: Chat sessions, each bound to one folder (a repository checkout or a worktree) and holding one or more agents. A new session is named after the folder's checked-out branch, like its worktree in the sidebar (or the folder name without one), and can be renamed. Agents added by hand are called Agent; agents started by another agent get the name it gives. Closing a session stops its agents and removes it; their transcripts stay on disk for the History menu. Each agent is its own conversation with its own agent process and session loop; its live state (messages, busy, queued messages, permissions, plan, mode, model, cost, input) is a Chat in app-state. Sessions, agent names and each agent's provider session id are saved in ~/.config/workbench/chat_sessions.json, so the conversations resume after a restart; a folder can have no session, and then the chat shows a New session button and actions that prompt the agent start one. Creating a worktree or a branch, or pressing New session, starts a new session, and agents are added with the chat's + tab or started by another agent. A project-level session belongs to a project instead of one folder: its agent works in the folder that holds the project's repositories, is listed under the project in the sidebar, and is shown in the chat while the project view is open (New project session starts one). An agent started from the chat on a named provider or model saves them with the agent, so it keeps running on them after a restart.

node.title: Claims (branch work overlap)
node.description: Derives the blast radius of intent work from git, without storing anything: the nodes a graph diff changes, the files those nodes own, and the nodes that link to them. open_claims reads every other branch with commits HEAD doesn't have, and builds each branch's claim from its graph diffed against the merge base plus the code files it changed, together with the branch's authors. overlaps compares the local pending changes with those claims, so contention shows up before any agent runs.

node.title: Intent-conflict review
node.description: Shown instead of the graph while .workbench/graph.json has an unresolved git merge conflict. It merges the three merge stages per node: intent changed on one side only is taken as is, and a node or module whose intent both sides changed differently is listed as a conflict with both versions side by side (description, links, files) and the nodes that use it. A person picks mine or theirs for each one; nothing is merged automatically. Saving writes and stages the graph, resets conflicting nodes in the baseline to the common base so they show up as pending work, and offers a commit message with an Intent-Resolution trailer.

node.title: GitHub integration
node.description: Talks to GitHub through the gh CLI so the user can read, write, review and merge pull requests of this project and read related repositories for context. Its interface is the GitHub tab component plus the related-repos list in AppState, which the prompt builder turns into Workbench context.

node.title: GitHub tab
node.description: Container with a repository selector (this repo or any related repo), sub-tabs for Pull requests, New PR and Related repos, and a reload button. Shares the selected repo, open PR and a reload counter with its children through a context.

node.title: Pull request list
node.description: Lists up to 50 pull requests of the selected repository filtered by open, closed, merged or all, with state, number, title, author, branches and review decision. Clicking one opens its detail view.

node.title: PR detail, review & merge
node.description: Shows a pull request's description, checks, reviews and comments, and its diff on demand. Posts comments, approvals and change requests, and merges with squash, merge or rebase (optionally deleting the branch) behind a confirm step. Ask Workbench to review sends a read-only review prompt to the chat.

node.title: New pull request
node.description: Opens a pull request from the current branch into the base branch (the default branch unless changed), with title, markdown body and draft flag, optionally pushing the branch first. Refuses to open one from the base branch. Draft with Workbench asks Workbench to write the title and description from the branch's commits.

node.title: Related repositories
node.description: Adds and removes related repositories (owner/repo or a github.com URL), jumps to a related repo's pull requests, and browses its files through the contents API. A file can be added to the chat input as context, truncated to keep prompts small.

node.title: GitHub service (gh CLI)
node.description: Wraps the gh CLI with prompts disabled: current and named repo info, list, view and diff pull requests (diffs parsed by the git service's parser), create, comment, review and merge, and read repository contents and raw files. Repository names and content paths are validated before they reach gh.

node.title: Related repos file
node.description: .workbench/github.json holds the list of related repositories. It is loaded with the rest of the workbench data, and saving it bumps the system-prompt version so Workbench restarts with the new context.

node.title: GitHub CLI (gh)
node.description: The external gh executable, authenticated with gh auth login. It runs in the project directory and talks to the GitHub API.

node.title: MCP connections
node.description: Lets every provider call tools on MCP servers. The user configures servers (local stdio programs or remote http/sse URLs) in the MCP tab at two levels: their own servers in the user config folder, used in every project and kept across updates, and the project's servers in .workbench/mcp.json. A project server replaces a user server of the same name. The agent CLIs (Workbench Code, Codex, Vibe) get the active servers in their own config, and the API providers reach them through the MCP manager. Its interface is the MCP tab, the mcp_servers list in AppState and the MCP manager.

node.title: MCP tab
node.description: Lists the MCP servers in three parts. Integrations shows each preset server (such as Linear) as an on/off switch with its logo; on adds it as a project server and shows its sign-in and status. Below are your servers (all projects) and this project's custom servers, each with its own add button. A custom card is collapsed to its head row (enabled toggle, name, scope and delete buttons, status) and expands to its transport and either a command with arguments and environment lines or a URL with header lines and OAuth sign-in. A card can move between the two levels.

node.title: MCP server model
node.description: The Server type with its transport and scope (user or project), loading the user and project files into one list and saving each server back to its own file, and active(), the usable servers where a project server replaces a user server of the same name. claude_config turns the active servers into the mcpServers JSON for --mcp-config. KEY=value and Name: value lines become env and header objects, which the Codex and Vibe runners reuse for their own config formats. expand_env fills in ${VAR} references for the MCP manager. PRESETS lists the remote servers Workbench knows (name, URL and logo); a project server with a preset's name is shown as that preset's toggle.

node.title: MCP connections file
node.description: The project's MCP servers in .workbench/mcp.json. It is loaded with the rest of the workbench data and is committed with the project, so secrets should be written as ${ENV_VAR} references. It is only created once the project has a server.

node.title: User MCP servers file
node.description: mcp.json in the user's Workbench config folder holds the user's own MCP servers. It sits outside every project and outside the self-update checkout, so these servers are used in every project and survive app updates.

node.title: MCP servers
node.description: The external MCP servers. The agent CLI in use starts the stdio ones as subprocesses and connects to the http/sse ones, then exposes their tools to the agent.

node.title: MCP manager
node.description: Workbench's own MCP client, used by the API providers, which have no MCP support of their own. It keeps one connection per active server, shared by every chat, opens it the first time a turn asks for tools and reopens it when the server's config or project changes. It lists the tools as mcp__<server>__<tool> with their schemas and read-only hints, calls a tool and returns its text output. It uses the rmcp crate for stdio and streamable http servers; sse servers only work through the agent CLIs.

node.title: MCP OAuth sign-in
node.description: Signs in to remote MCP servers that use OAuth. sign_in opens the server's login page in the browser and waits for the redirect on a one-shot listener on 127.0.0.1; rmcp handles discovery, client registration, PKCE and the code exchange. Tokens are kept per server URL in mcp-oauth.json in the user's config folder, never in the project. Before each turn, with_tokens adds an Authorization: Bearer header to every signed-in server (refreshing the token when it is about to expire), so every provider gets a plain URL with a header.

node.title: LLM providers
node.description: Switches the chat between agent CLIs installed on this machine (Workbench, Codex, Mistral Vibe) and direct chat APIs (Anthropic, OpenAI, Mistral, OpenRouter). The chosen provider, a model per provider, API keys and loaded model lists are stored per user. Its interface is the header picker, the Providers tab and the Codex, Vibe and API runners the agent layer starts.

node.title: Provider & model picker
node.description: Settings controls for the provider and the model. Switching provider starts a new session, since sessions can't move between providers. Changing the model restarts the agent on the next message. The provider is a themed Dropdown and the model a ComboBox with the provider's model list as suggestions.

node.title: Providers tab
node.description: One card per provider, showing whether its CLI is installed or its API key is set, with a Use button. API providers get a key field and a Load models button that fetches the provider's live model list.

node.title: Provider catalogue & settings
node.description: The Provider enum: label, how it is reached (CLI binary or API base URL, key variable and API style), suggested models and availability. Settings holds the chosen provider, the model per provider, typed API keys (the environment variable wins) and loaded model lists.

node.title: Provider settings file
node.description: providers.json in the user's Workbench config folder, outside every project, so API keys are never committed.

node.title: Codex runner
node.description: Builds one `codex exec --json` turn (resume, model, sandbox from the chat mode, Workbench instructions as developer_instructions, MCP servers as -c overrides) and parses its JSONL events into chat events: thread id, messages, commands, file changes, MCP and web-search calls, and turn end or failure.

node.title: Vibe runner
node.description: Builds one `vibe -p --output streaming` turn (resume, agent from the chat mode, model and MCP servers through VIBE_* variables, Workbench instructions at the top of a new session's first prompt) and parses its history entries into chat events, skipping the entries a resumed session replays. node.title: API chat client

node.title: Codex CLI
node.description: The external `codex` executable from OpenAI, run once per message in the project folder.

node.title: Mistral Vibe CLI
node.description: The external `vibe` executable from Mistral, run once per message in the project folder.

node.title: Provider APIs
node.description: The HTTP APIs of Anthropic, OpenAI, Mistral and OpenRouter, called with the user's API keys.

node.title: MCP tools for API providers
node.description: The API chat client gets the tools of the active MCP servers from the MCP manager, offers them to the model and calls them when the model asks.

Review diff and ask Workbench about a hunk
Review and merge a pull request

node.title: Intent ledger
node.description: The append-only log in .workbench/ledger.ndjson, the source of truth for the graph. When an agent edits a description, the edit becomes a proposal that a person accepts or rejects (verdict). Workbench refuses to append if earlier lines were changed or dropped (extends). node.title: Blast-radius enforcement

node.title: Work orders

node.title: Verification before absorb

node.title: workbench-check library

For plain chat turns of an agent in the open folder it snapshots the graph when the turn starts and, when the turn succeeds, moves the graph edits Workbench made into the baseline (the whole graph if it was in sync, otherwise only Workbench's changes), so they don't show up as the user's pending changes. Every graph load, outside change and edit is recorded in the intent ledger. Description proposals are accepted or rejected through it. A scoped run snapshots its blast radius when it starts and is enforced when it finishes. An agent's node changes are absorbed only after verification passes. focus_node selects a node and asks the canvas to zoom to it, and live_edits_of gives the files a scoped run is editing that a node claims. One long-running loop per agent that receives that agent's Cmd values (Send, Prompt, Interrupt, Restart, Resume, Close; Close stops the agent and ends the loop) and owns its live agent, so agents in a session work at the same time. With Workbench it spawns the agent process lazily in the agent's folder, respawns it when the rules version changes, and resumes the agent's stored session id. A generation counter drops events from killed processes. Streamed events become the agent's chat items; when the agent works in the open folder, file-touching tool results bump repo_version and reload the open file, and Done settles its chat turn or graph job against the baseline. A reply that ends with focus blocks has them stripped and shown as node choices in the chat, and a single match is focused on the graph right away. Tool results of a scoped run are recorded as its live edits. A reply that ends with spawn-agent blocks starts those agents with their tasks: in the same session, or, when a block names a repository of the agent's project, in a new session in that repository. A project-level agent gets the project's repositories as its context instead of the open folder's graph. Changing a project's repositories or descriptions also restarts Workbench with the updated project context. When it spawns the agent it passes the enabled MCP connections as --mcp-config, and the MCP statuses from the agent's init event go to app-state. With any other provider every message starts a new turn through the agent layer, and only Workbench session ids are saved for resuming. Each agent runs on its own provider and model when it was started on one (AppState::agent_provider), otherwise on the ones in the settings; a spawn-agent block can name a provider and model for the new agent, and an unknown provider id is shown as an error instead of starting it. Finds the agent binary, then spawns it with stream-json input/output, partial messages, the permission mode of the chat mode, AskUserQuestion turned off (the agent asks in its reply instead), an optional --resume, --model, --append-system-prompt and --mcp-config. It writes user messages, interrupt control requests and permission answers (a plan approval also sets the session's mode) to stdin. Stdout lines are parsed into AgentEvent values (Init with the MCP server statuses, TextDelta, ToolUse, ToolResult, Done, Stderr, Exited) and tagged with a generation number. Also provides tool summaries and file-path extraction. ClaudeProcess implements the AgentAdapter trait. Event shapes it doesn't know, and CLI versions outside TESTED_CLI_VERSIONS (2.1.322, pinned by a recorded fixture), come back as Unsupported events and are shown in the chat.

Builds every structured prompt sent to Workbench: generate or refresh the architecture graph (with the JSON schema, including modules), draft nodes into the network the user is looking at, process graph changes into code edits (new, removed and edited modules and attachments included; Workbench may add nodes for new units it had to create, and is told which nodes and files other branches are also changing), debug a flow (several modes), audit code against rules, ask about a node, review a pull request, and the per-session system-prompt append, which tells Workbench to keep the graph in step with every code change (files, new nodes for new units, removed nodes, updated descriptions and links), plus, when the open folder belongs to a project, the project's name and the other repositories (folder, GitHub name, description) Workbench may read, the modules guide, enabled rules and the related GitHub repositories. Builds every structured prompt sent to Workbench: generate or refresh the architecture graph (with the JSON schema, including modules), draft nodes into the network the user is looking at, process graph changes into code edits (new, removed and edited modules and attachments included; Workbench may add nodes for new units it had to create, and is told which nodes and files other branches are also changing), debug a flow (several modes), audit code against rules, ask about a node, review a pull request, and the per-session system-prompt append, which tells Workbench to keep the graph in step with every code change (files, new nodes for new units, removed nodes, updated descriptions and links), plus, when the open folder belongs to a project, the project's name and the other repositories (folder, GitHub name, description) Workbench may read, the modules guide, enabled rules and the related GitHub repositories. Every agent is also told how to start more agents in its session: a spawn-agent block with a name and the full task, which spawn_requests parses out of the reply. It also builds the project-level agent's prompt (the project and its repositories) and the spawn-agent instructions, which name the project's repositories an agent can start another agent in. The spawn-agent instructions also list every provider id with its models, so when the user names a provider or model in the chat ("use vibe large 4 to build X") the agent adds provider and model to the block. The Process prompt is built from typed work orders, each with its own instruction and declared blast radius. Agents with a graph are also told to answer any request to see or find a feature ("show me X", "where is X", "what handles X?") quickly from the graph, without searching the code first, and to end the reply with focus blocks naming the responsible nodes and a confidence, which focus_requests parses out of the reply; after changing code they add blocks for the nodes they changed. They are also told to find code through the intent query command first and to search the file system only for what the graph doesn't cover.

Collapsible list on the left of every project with its repositories and worktrees, read from the projects saved in ~/.config/workbench/projects.json. Under each repository and worktree it lists its chat sessions, with a dot while one of their agents works and a ✕ on hover that closes the session; clicking the name of the open session renames it. Any session can be closed, and a folder without sessions shows a New session button instead. Under each session it lists its agents with their provider's logo and name and their state (working, waiting, or needs you when a permission or plan waits for an answer). Clicking a session or an agent opens its folder and shows it in the chat. Under each project it also lists coding agents running outside Workbench, with their provider's logo, the folder they run in and whether they are working or waiting for a prompt. Clicking a project shows its project view; clicking a repository, worktree or agent opens that folder. It can create a project and add a repository to a project. A project's project-level sessions are listed right under its name. Each project, repository, worktree and session with agents has a ▾ in front of it that folds away the rows under it; the folded rows are saved in ~/.config/workbench/sidebar_collapsed.json. A worktree row has an ✕ that asks whether to close the worktree (delete its folder with git worktree remove and close its chat sessions; the branch stays) or just hide it from the sidebar; the project view's worktree list can show a hidden one again.

Conversation view of the agent the chat shows: user messages, labelled prompts, streaming assistant markdown, tool calls with results, info lines and errors. The input box sends Cmd::Send and has a Stop button for Cmd::Interrupt while busy. ChatTabs, in the chat's top bar next to “Chat”, shows the session's title and one tab per agent with its provider's logo (and a dot while it works and ! while it waits for an answer); clicking a tab switches the chat to that agent, hovering it shows an ✕ on its left that closes the agent (closing the last one closes the session), and + adds an agent. In a project view the session title in the top bar is a session picker: the project's own sessions, every session in its repositories and their worktrees, and + New project session. Picking a repository's session shows it without leaving the project view. A reply that names responsible nodes shows them as buttons with the agent's confidence; clicking one focuses it on the graph. File references in messages (a path, path:line or path:line:col) are links: clicking one opens the file in the editor at that line, hovering shows its size, and a path in backticks that doesn't exist is shown struck through. A plan waiting for approval takes the height it needs, up to most of the chat, and scrolls inside past that.

Mounts the bundled CodeMirror 6 editor (vim mode, many languages) in the webview through document.eval. Load and focus messages go to JS; Change, Save (:w), Close (:q) and Reload (:e) messages come back and update the open file in AppState. The editor keeps Esc to itself, so on macOS it doesn't reach the window and leave full screen.

The chat floats over the graph, code or rules view, at the bottom centre until it is first moved. Dragging its top bar moves it anywhere in the window, even partly past the right and bottom edges, as long as the bar stays in the window; dragging its edges resizes it, and the place and size are saved. A press in the graph fades the chat to a peek at the latest reply unless the Lock toggle is on; a locked chat stays open even if it was faded before it was locked. Moves are limited by the page size as the webview measures it, so the chat reaches every edge on wide monitors. Detach moves the chat into a window of its own and Attach puts it back; on macOS, detaching from a full-screen window leaves full screen first. Its top bar holds the agent tabs of the chat session it shows; when the open folder has no session it shows a New session button instead. While a plan waits for approval the chat grows to most of the window height, anchored at the bottom, so the plan has room.

Finds the agent binary, then spawns it with stream-json input/output, partial messages, the permission mode of the chat mode, AskUserQuestion turned off (the agent asks in its reply instead), an optional --resume, --model, --append-system-prompt and --mcp-config. It writes user messages, interrupt control requests and permission answers (a plan approval also sets the session's mode) to stdin. Stdout lines are parsed into AgentEvent values (Init with the MCP server statuses, TextDelta, ToolUse, ToolResult, Done, Stderr, Exited) and tagged with a generation number. Also provides tool summaries and file-path extraction. ClaudeProcess implements the AgentAdapter trait. Event shapes it doesn't know come back as Unsupported events and are shown in the chat.

node.title: Link routing
node.description: Works out the path of every link on the graph canvas, Floorplan style: links leave a node's right side and enter the next node's left side, turning only at right angles with rounded corners. Ports are spread down each side in the order of the other ends, and all links into one node share a vertical trunk just left of it, so they stack into one path. A link passes every column between its ends through a gap between two nodes, stepping up or down in the space between columns, so no link is drawn through a node. Backward links that close a cycle travel leftwards the same way.

decisions.decision: Links are routed orthogonally (right angles, rounded corners) with a shared trunk per target, modelled on Floorplan's ELK layered layout with ORTHOGONAL edge routing
decisions.why: Floorplan's graphs are easier to read: no lines crossing everywhere, and links into the same node stack into the same path
decisions.instead_of: cubic Bezier curves straight from source to target

decisions.decision: A small router of our own in Rust instead of ELK
decisions.why: There is no ELK for Rust, and our nodes keep user-pinned positions, so routes must work for any placement, not only a layout ELK computed
decisions.instead_of: embedding elkjs and letting it place and route

decisions.decision: Links cross each column through a gap between its nodes, jogging in the space between columns, and backward links do the same leftwards
decisions.why: The project graph has real backward links (22 of 175 root links close a cycle, mostly into app-state, session-loop and chat-sessions), and long or backward links must never be drawn through nodes
decisions.instead_of: one horizontal detour above or below everything the link spans

decisions.decision: Links into different targets keep a lane apart in a gap when a free lane is near, and otherwise share the nearest lane
decisions.why: A gap between rows only holds about two lanes; sharing reads better than a long loop round the whole column, and searching only the nearby gaps keeps routing fast (about 44 ms for 1500 nodes and 4000 links)
decisions.instead_of: always finding a free lane, which sent links round whole columns and took 200 ms on big graphs

patch.description: Conversation view of the agent the chat shows: user messages, labelled prompts, streaming assistant markdown, tool calls with results, info lines and errors. The input box sends Cmd::Send and has a Stop button for Cmd::Interrupt while busy. ChatTabs, in the chat's top bar next to “Chat”, shows the session's title and one tab per agent with its provider's logo (and a dot while it works and ! while it waits for an answer); clicking a tab switches the chat to that agent, hovering it shows an ✕ on its left that closes the agent (closing the last one closes the session), and + adds an agent. In a project view the session title in the top bar is a session picker: the project's own sessions, every session in its repositories and their worktrees, and + New project session. Picking a repository's session shows it without leaving the project view. A reply that names responsible nodes shows them as buttons with the agent's confidence; clicking one focuses it on the graph. File references in messages (a path, path:line or path:line:col) are links: clicking one opens the file in the editor at that line, hovering shows its size, and a path in backticks that doesn't exist is shown struck through. After each finished turn, a folded “changed files” row lists the files the turn's edit tool calls wrote; opened, each file shows its uncommitted diff against HEAD and unfolds to its hunks.

patch.description: One long-running loop per agent that receives that agent's Cmd values (Send, Prompt, Interrupt, Restart, Resume, Close; Close stops the agent and ends the loop) and owns its live agent, so agents in a session work at the same time. With Workbench it spawns the agent process lazily in the agent's folder, respawns it when the rules version changes, and resumes the agent's stored session id. A generation counter drops events from killed processes. Streamed events become the agent's chat items; when the agent works in the open folder, file-touching tool results bump repo_version and reload the open file, and Done settles its chat turn or graph job against the baseline. A reply that ends with focus blocks has them stripped and shown as node choices in the chat, and a single match is focused on the graph right away. Tool results of a scoped run are recorded as its live edits. A reply that ends with spawn-agent blocks starts those agents with their tasks: in the same session, or, when a block names a repository of the agent's project, in a new session in that repository. A project-level agent gets the project's repositories as its context instead of the open folder's graph. Changing a project's repositories or descriptions also restarts Workbench with the updated project context. When it spawns the agent it passes the enabled MCP connections as --mcp-config, and the MCP statuses from the agent's init event go to app-state. With any other provider every message starts a new turn through the agent layer, and only Workbench session ids are saved for resuming. Each agent runs on its own provider and model when it was started on one (AppState::agent_provider), otherwise on the ones in the settings; a spawn-agent block can name a provider and model for the new agent, and an unknown provider id is shown as an error instead of starting it. The provider and model of a turn come from agent_provider. A job's route wins over the agent's own provider. When a turn fails because the provider ran out of tokens and a fallback is set, the agent moves to the fallback and gets the recent conversation as its next prompt. After a successful turn the files it changed that no node owns are named in the chat. A discussion chat's loop runs read only in Plan with Edit, Write, NotebookEdit and ExitPlanMode disallowed, denies every permission request, prefixes each message with an <execution_chat> digest of its execution chat (new items since the last message plus its state), and skips turn tracking, spawn blocks and plan approval.

Builds every structured prompt sent to Workbench: generate or refresh the architecture graph (with the JSON schema, including modules), draft nodes into the network the user is looking at, process graph changes into code edits (new, removed and edited modules and attachments included; Workbench may add nodes for new units it had to create, and is told which nodes and files other branches are also changing), debug a flow (several modes), audit code against rules, ask about a node, review a pull request, and the per-session system-prompt append, which tells Workbench to keep the graph in step with every code change (files, new nodes for new units, removed nodes, updated descriptions and links), plus, when the open folder belongs to a project, the project's name and the other repositories (folder, GitHub name, description) Workbench may read, the modules guide, enabled rules and the related GitHub repositories. Every agent is also told how to start more agents in its session: a spawn-agent block with a name and the full task, which spawn_requests parses out of the reply. It also builds the project-level agent's prompt (the project and its repositories) and the spawn-agent instructions, which name the project's repositories an agent can start another agent in. The spawn-agent instructions also list every provider id with its models, so when the user names a provider or model in the chat ("use vibe large 4 to build X") the agent adds provider and model to the block. The Process prompt is built from typed work orders, each with its own instruction and declared blast radius. Agents with a graph are also told to answer any request to see or find a feature ("show me X", "where is X", "what handles X?") quickly from the graph, without searching the code first, and to end the reply with focus blocks naming the responsible nodes and a confidence, which focus_requests parses out of the reply; after changing code they add blocks for the nodes they changed. They are also told to find code through the intent query command first and to search the file system only for what the graph doesn't cover. The graph rules tell agents that nodes standing for the same thing share one name (naming::prompt_rule).

Lists the field-level differences between the current graph and the baseline, including nodes inside modules (labelled with their module) and added, removed or edited modules. Show opens the right module and selects the node. Before processing it reads the claims of the other git branches and warns when they change the same nodes or files, or nodes these changes depend on; the user can process anyway or process only the changes no other branch touches. With an optional note, it sends a Process job that asks Workbench to change the code to match the edited graph. When the job succeeds, the baseline is updated. Description changes are flagged. Descriptions that agents proposed are listed for the user to accept or reject. Possibly stale dependents are shown, and a Strict toggle makes out-of-scope edits get undone. Each proposal lists the description sentences it adds and removes. A naming list (PRO-245) shows nodes that stand for the same module or reference under different titles, with a button to give them the canonical name.

The window body under the header: the projects sidebar on the left and the workbench on the right. The workbench switches between the Graph, Code and Rules views, shows workbench load errors, and shows the project view when a project is picked. The layout (sidebar open, node menu width and open state, chat anchor, expanded and locked) is saved in ~/.config/workbench/layout.json. Above the main view, a ledger banner lists ledger changes that came in from outside while the app ran, and warns when the ledger watcher stops.

The Code pane's MCP tab and the MCP servers every provider can call. The user manages MCP servers at two levels in the tab: their own servers, used in every project, and the project's servers. Every active one goes to Claude Code (--mcp-config), Codex (-c mcp_servers) or Vibe (VIBE_MCP_SERVERS), and the API providers call them through Workbench's own MCP manager. The reported connection status is shown back in the tab. Remote servers that use OAuth (such as Linear) are signed in from the tab, and each turn passes their token on as a header.

Lets the user switch the chat between Claude Code, Codex and Mistral Vibe (agent CLIs) and the Anthropic, OpenAI, Mistral and OpenRouter APIs, with a model per provider. The header uses it for the provider and model picker, the Code pane for the Providers tab, and the agent layer to run Codex, Vibe and API turns. The provider picked in the settings is only the default: an agent can be started on another provider and model from the chat through a spawn-agent block, and the chat tab, sidebar row and mode toggle show the agent's own provider. A fallback provider and model can be set for when a chat's provider runs out of tokens; the chat then continues there with the conversation so far.

The chat floats over the graph, code or rules view, at the bottom centre until it is first moved. Dragging its top bar moves it anywhere in the window, even partly past the right and bottom edges, as long as the bar stays in the window; dragging its edges resizes it, and the place and size are saved. A press in the graph fades the chat to a peek at the latest reply unless the Lock toggle is on; a locked chat stays open even if it was faded before it was locked. Moves are limited by the page size as the webview measures it, so the chat reaches every edge on wide monitors. Detach moves the chat into a window of its own and Attach puts it back; on macOS, detaching from a full-screen window leaves full screen first. Its top bar holds the agent tabs of the chat session it shows; when the open folder has no session it shows a New session button instead. Next to the agent tabs, in the dock and the detached window, ChatViewToggle switches between Execute and Discuss, with a dot when the hidden side works.

Finds the coding agents (Claude Code, Codex, Vibe) running on this machine outside Workbench by reading /proc, which folder each runs in, and whether it is working (using CPU) or waiting for a prompt. Every agent is given to the project repository or worktree it runs in; Workbench's own agents are shown with their chat sessions instead. Each agent kind and each provider maps to its LLM company's logo (Claude, OpenAI, Mistral, OpenRouter), drawn from Simple Icons path data. The worktree list in the project view can add a worktree, which also starts a new chat session in it.

Chat sessions, each bound to one folder (a repository checkout or a worktree) and holding one or more agents. A new session is named after the folder's checked-out branch, like its worktree in the sidebar (or the folder name without one), and can be renamed. Agents added by hand are called Agent; agents started by another agent get the name it gives. Closing a session stops its agents and removes it; their transcripts stay on disk for the History menu. Each agent is its own conversation with its own agent process and session loop; its live state (messages, busy, queued messages, permissions, plan, mode, model, cost, input) is a Chat in app-state. Sessions, agent names and each agent's provider session id are saved in ~/.config/workbench/chat_sessions.json, so the conversations resume after a restart; a folder can have no session, and then the chat shows a New session button and actions that prompt the agent start one. Creating a worktree or a branch, or pressing New session, starts a new session, and agents are added with the chat's + tab or started by another agent. A project-level session belongs to a project instead of one folder: its agent works in the folder that holds the project's repositories, is listed under the project in the sidebar, and is shown in the chat while the project view is open (New project session starts one). An agent started from the chat on a named provider or model saves them with the agent, so it keeps running on them after a restart. Each agent can also have a discussion chat (PRO-248): a second, read-only Chat with its own session loop, started on first use, kept in AppState.discussions (not in the session's agents) and resumed from SavedAgent.discussion. chat_view says which of the two the chat window shows.

The append-only log in .workbench/ledger.ndjson, the source of truth for the graph. Every entry is a ULID-stamped op from a closed set (node.add, node.merge, node.remove, ref.add, flow.put, flow.remove, tombstone), attributed to a person, an agent or an edit from outside. record diffs the materialized ledger against graph.json and appends the ops that explain the difference. materialize rebuilds the graph from the entries and takes positions from graph.json. When an agent edits a description, the edit becomes a proposal that a person accepts or rejects (verdict). Workbench refuses to append if earlier lines were changed or dropped (extends). The frozen schema is in docs/ledger-spec.md. ledger::record adopts entries someone else appended since the ledger was last read (PRO-246): it rebases the writer's own changes onto the ledger on disk instead of diffing a stale graph against it, and returns the merged graph and any field both sides changed. app::watch_ledger polls the ledger's size and modification time every 2 seconds while the app runs, and the Workbench layout's banner lists what came in, the conflicts, and a warning when the watcher stops.

Lets every provider call tools on MCP servers. The user configures servers (local stdio programs or remote http/sse URLs) in the MCP tab at two levels: their own servers in the user config folder, used in every project and kept across updates, and the project's servers in .workbench/mcp.json. A project server replaces a user server of the same name. The agent CLIs (Claude Code, Codex, Vibe) get the active servers in their own config, and the API providers reach them through the MCP manager. Its interface is the MCP tab, the mcp_servers list in AppState and the MCP manager.

decisions.decision: Nodes and modules carry `decisions` (decision, why, instead_of, source, date) and `invariants` next to the description
decisions.instead_of: only a free-text description that mixes what and why
decisions.why: The graph should show how and why the app was steered, not only what each part does, so it is more than a pretty map

decisions.decision: Added figma to the known node kinds, with Figma's orange as its colour
decisions.why: The user wants a Figma node as its own kind of node on the graph

decisions.decision: surface_hash covers kind, title, description and invariants, hashed with FNV-1a and prefixed with a version (`v1:`)
decisions.instead_of: std's DefaultHasher, whose output can change between Rust versions
decisions.why: Files, links and decisions are internal, so refactors behind a surface don't flag consumers; the hash is stored on disk so it must be stable across builds, and the version prefix makes a future change of the hashed fields show as changed instead of silently matching

decisions.decision: References can only pick nodes the other project marks as exported surfaces, never its internal nodes
decisions.instead_of: picking any node of the referenced graph
decisions.why: Otherwise upstream refactors break every downstream graph and the graph stops being a stable abstraction

decisions.decision: Each picked node stores the surface hash it was built against, and a mismatch shows the same warning ring as branch conflicts
decisions.why: Answers what this talks to and whether the other side changed, using the visual language users already know from ghost branches

invariants: References only point at exported surfaces, never internal nodes

patch.description: Serde types Node, Flow, Module and Graph, plus helpers: lookup, unique ids, slugify, node removal, edges, auto-layout into columns, kind colours, and diff(base, current), which produces field-level Change records. A Module is an isolated node network stored in graph.modules; a node whose `module` field names it is an attachment point, and one module can be attached in many places (never inside itself). The diff covers the main network, every module network and module title/description, tagging each change with its scope. absorb applies a set of changes from a current graph onto a baseline. load and save read and write the graph JSON under .workbench. A node with `export: true` is an exported surface that other projects may reference; surface_hash fingerprints its kind, title, description and invariants as a versioned `v1:` FNV-1a hash.

Nodes of kind `reference` point outside the project through `reference.source`: a local folder or file, a GitHub repository (URL, owner/repo or github:owner/repo@ref/path), a website, or an npm/crate/pypi/go package. Sources are parsed into a Source, and Workbench looks for the referenced project's .workbench/graph.json: locally by walking up from the path, on GitHub through gh at the path and its parents, or in node_modules and the cargo registry for packages. Loaded graphs are cached in AppState by source. The user can pick nodes that the other project exports (`export: true`) into `reference.nodes`; each pick stores the node's surface hash, and drift compares it with the other side so a reference whose surface changed, stopped being exported or disappeared gets a warning ring on the canvas and an Accept new surface button in the inspector. Picked descriptions and files, with any drift warning, are put into the system prompt, the selection context and process prompts as read-only context.
